n: Gideon’s army camps at the spring of Harod, with the Midianites spread out in the valley below near the hill of Moreh.

f.g: A hill on the north side of the Jezreel valley.

n: Surprisingly, God says Gideon’s army is too big. If Israel won with a large force, they would boast that they saved themselves. God wants the victory to be clearly His.

f.w: Mine own hand hath saved me

n: Following the law of Moses, anyone afraid may go home. Twenty-two thousand leave; ten thousand remain.

f.g: Puzzling, since Gilead lies east of the Jordan; some suggest a local hill or a copying change.

n: Still too many. God will test the men at the water and choose who goes.

f.g: Test, sift — as metal is refined.

n: At the water, the men are separated by how they drink: those who lap like a dog and those who kneel down.
Only three hundred lapped water from their hands; everyone else knelt to drink. The point is not their skill — God simply chose the smallest group.

f.w: putting their hand to their mouth
f.g: Scooping water to the mouth while staying alert.

n: God declares He will save Israel with just three hundred men. The others go home.
The three hundred keep the departing men’s supplies and trumpets — which will be their only “weapons.” Midian waits below.
That night God tells Gideon to attack, for the victory is already given.

f.g: Spoken as already done — the certainty of God’s promise.

n: Knowing Gideon’s fear, God offers encouragement: if you’re afraid, take your servant Phurah and go scout the camp.

f.g: God meets Gideon where he is, without scolding.

n: Gideon will hear something that strengthens him. He and Phurah creep to the edge of the enemy camp.
The enemy army fills the valley like locusts, their camels like the sand of the seashore.

f.w: as the sand by the sea side

n: A soldier tells his dream: a round loaf of barley bread rolled into camp and flattened a tent. Barley was a poor farmer’s grain — a picture of humble Israel.

f.g: Barley was cheaper than wheat, food of the poor; Israel was the farming people, Midian the tent-dwellers.

n: His friend interprets: it is the sword of Gideon. Even the enemy knows God has given Midian to Israel.

f.w: into his hand hath God delivered Midian

n: Gideon’s first response is to worship. Then he returns, transformed, and rouses his men: the Lord has given you victory.
Gideon divides his men into three companies, giving each a ram’s horn and a clay jar with a torch hidden inside.
“Watch me and do what I do.” Gideon leads by example.

f.w: Look on me, and do likewise

n: At his signal, they will all blow their horns and shout, “The sword of the LORD, and of Gideon!” God’s name comes first.
They reach the camp just after the guard changes at the middle watch, around midnight, when sentries are least settled. They blow horns and smash jars.

f.g: The second of three night watches, around 10 p.m. to 2 a.m.

n: Torches flare as the jars break; three hundred horns blare; the shout rings out. In the dark it sounds like a vast army.
Israel’s men simply stand in place, and the enemy camp panics and runs.

f.w: stood every man in his place

n: In confusion, the Lord sets the enemies against each other. They flee east toward the Jordan.

f.w: set every man's sword against his fellow

n: Men from the northern tribes join in pursuing the fleeing Midianites.
Gideon calls Ephraim to block the Jordan crossings, cutting off escape.

f.g: Seize the fords and streams ahead of them.

n: Ephraim captures and kills two Midianite princes, Oreb (“raven”) and Zeeb (“wolf”). Later scripture remembers this as a great deliverance.
